source.title: Decoding Alignment without Encoding Alignment: A critique of similarity analysis in neuroscience
source.authors: Johannes Bertram; Luciano Dyballa; T. Keller; Savik Kinger; Steven W. Zucker

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Its printed title, “Decoding Alignment without Encoding Alignment: A Missing Component for Interpretability,” differs from the supplied metadata title.
record.tranche_reason: The paper presents controlled results arguing that decoding-based similarity metrics can remain high despite changes to internal functional organization, and that metric choice can change the apparent result. This refines the scope of similarity-based alignment claims; it does not test convergence with scale or cross-modal convergence.
record.gate_note: The study tests metric sensitivity and the limits of decoding-based alignment scores, not convergence across model scale, independently trained architectures, or image-caption pairs. Rows cover its MNIST metric comparisons and selected reported subpopulation comparisons. Cited findings from other work, task accuracy, attribution and circuit-structure measures, and blur robustness are not rows because they do not themselves measure a claim-version similarity result.
record.test_reason: In a controlled MNIST experiment, CNNs trained with and without a clustering loss look nearly identical under RSA, CKA and Procrustes (about 0.96) but differ sharply under GW encoding similarity (0.50). Measured cross-model similarity thus depends on the metric chosen, which bears on V6. The FPS subpopulation analyses compare subsets of one system with its full population, not separate models, so they do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say decoding-based metrics (RSA, CKA, Procrustes) reflect readout similarity, not internal functional organization. They recommend pairing them with encoding manifolds and GW similarity.
record.recipe_differences: This is a critique using controlled changes to encoding topology and comparisons among decoding and encoding metrics; it does not reproduce a scale-convergence or cross-modal convergence method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with metric, clustering-loss strength, subpopulation topology, and model or dataset. The text reports k-NN as an exception among otherwise often near-ceiling correlation-based measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Small or locally clustered subpopulations reproduce the full population's RSA, CKA and Procrustes scores near ceiling, regardless of encoding-manifold topology. This holds across retina, V1, Allen areas and ML models; k-NN accuracy is the exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoding-based similarity scores can be matched by small, non-representative subpopulations, so high alignment does not imply shared internal organization.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented at the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2026; the text also states it appears at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning.
record.problems: The controlled MNIST result uses a specific clustering loss and a relatively shallow network; the authors say the loss changes tuning sharpness and connectivity simultaneously, and an ablation isolating topology from direct regularizer effects remains future work. They also state that GW has not yet been validated against ground-truth circuit differences in cross-system model–brain comparisons. The MNIST controlled comparison has 20 seeds per condition; many Table 4 values are means and standard deviations over 5 FPS seeds.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional Table 4 dataset-by-metric comparisons, population-fraction sweeps (Figures 3 and 6), and PC-based subpopulation comparisons (Figures 9–11). These are not exhaustively itemized; rows prioritize the controlled MNIST comparison, metric-sensitive cases, and selected model/dataset results within the 60-row cap. The paper’s aggregate text result across systems is recorded in r17.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep across independently trained architectures.
No vision-language or paired image-caption comparison.
Seed-to-seed shared features or subspaces are not assessed.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
No recurrence of features or circuits across models.
Neighbour-count or other metric hyperparameters, stimulus-set dependence of a cross-model comparison, and out-of-distribution inputs.
Plateaus, and shared data or objectives as causes of convergence.

missing.what: λ=0.5, 1 and 10 sweep values (e.g. λ=10: RSA 0.968, CKA 0.982, Procrustes 0.981, GW 0.466; λ=0.5: GW 0.941).
Task accuracy held at about 0.985 across λ; the models differ in attribution entropy, assortativity and blur robustness.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a metric critique, not a convergence study. Its only cross-model comparison is MNIST CNNs trained under different losses; GW there measures encoding-manifold (neuron-space) similarity, a related but different construct from stimulus-space representational similarity. The V6 support should be read with that caveat. Table 1 does not explain how the baseline-column values (e.g. GW 0.958) are computed.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep of alignment between independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No paired image-caption or vision-language model comparison.
The MNIST models use different training conditions, but the paper does not test seed-to-seed shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No recurrence of interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits is assessed.

The study compares decoding metrics and selected subpopulation settings, but does not systematically vary stimulus datasets for the same alignment comparison, test similarity-metric hyperparameters such as neighbour count, or assess out-of-distribution inputs as an alignment measure.

The paper shows that matched decoding scores can coexist with different internal organization, but does not test whether shared training data or objectives explain cross-model convergence or whether alignment plateaus.

relationships.condition: MNIST CNNs trained with vs without clustering loss (λ sweep), decoding metrics vs GW encoding similarity
relationships.reason: RSA, CKA and Procrustes stay near 0.96 while GW falls to 0.50 at λ=10 (r1–r4). Up to λ=5 decoding scores barely move while GW drops to 0.706 (r5–r12); at λ=50 the values are 0.90–0.94 vs 0.28 (r13–r16).
relationships.display_finding: RSA, CKA and Procrustes stayed near 0.96 while GW fell to 0.50 at λ=10; through λ=5, decoding scores barely changed while GW reached 0.706, and at λ=50, decoding scores were 0.90–0.94 versus GW of 0.28.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The controlled MNIST comparison and settings where decoding metrics differ from the encoding-side score
reader_labels.reason: Changing clustering strength yields markedly different RSA/CKA/Procrustes and GW trajectories (r4, r8, r12–r16); Table 4 also shows some metric- and model-dependent changes (r18, r21–r22, r24–r32).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: RSA, CKA, and Procrustes in the MNIST λ=10 comparison and high-scoring correlation metrics across several FPS conditions
reader_labels.reason: Several decoding metrics are statistically unchanged or remain high despite altered encoding topology, so the metric dependence is not a uniform disappearance of measured similarity (r1–r3, r17, r19–r20, r23, r32).
